title: Google's AMIE Chatbot Interviewed 98 Boston Primary Care Patients Under Doctor Supervision Without a Single Safety Stop
key_facts: Google's research chatbot AMIE interviewed 98 patients by text before urgent primary-care visits at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC) in Boston; the study was published on 8 Oct 2026 in The Lancet.
Seven board-certified internal medicine physicians watched each conversation live by video; the team set four rules in advance for stopping a chat, and none of the 98 conversations met any of them.

The researchers reported one hallucination (a made-up statement) and one interaction a physician rated somewhat harmful, because the patient may have become anxious after AMIE raised lymphoma as a possible diagnosis.

AMIE's list of possible diagnoses included the doctor's final diagnosis 90% of the time (Google's summary); in blinded comparisons it performed similarly to primary care physicians on diagnosis and management plans, while doctors scored better on practical, cost-conscious care.
Patients' views of AI improved and most would use AMIE again, but fewer than half felt it would keep their information confidential or seemed honest and trustworthy.

Of 1,452 urgent visits scheduled, 140 eligible patients consented and 98 completed both the chat and the visit; emergency, pregnant and mental-health patients were excluded; no comparison group; single clinic.

Funded by Alphabet, Google's parent company; one BIDMC author was a visiting researcher at Google during part of the work. AMIE is a research system, not available to the public or approved for clinical use.
quote_evidence: None of the 98 analyzed conversations met any of those criteria.
The study was designed to test feasibility and safety, not to prove that AI improves health.
AMIE is a research system and is not available to the public or approved for clinical use.
why_it_matters_hint: One of the first real-world tests of a patient-facing diagnostic AI inside a working clinic, but it tested feasibility and safety only, not whether care improves.
